What we talk about are just things to be aware of You do not have to commit to anything you hear about today Successful programs are built with passion, not burnout Some ideas can help you right away, and maybe others are for later on, or maybe not for you at all, and that’s fine

documents.s: FIRST Lego League And FIRST Tech Challenge

documents.t: FIRST has programs for all ages of youth FRC - FIRST Robotics Competition: mostly high school FTC - FIRST Tech Challenge: middle school in MI, middle and high school elsewhere FLL: FIRST Lego League, mostly elementary in the USA, all youth ages internationally Split into K-3 and 4-5 programs in Michigan There’s also a pre-K version that’s sunsetting FLL is actually much larger than FRC

Season is September-December for most teams Detroit has dozens of teams at all levels Various groups and individuals support the teams, such as the Motor City Alliance, DHDC, Team 503 Frog Force, UDM, and of course the MEZ Teams meet at their schools and on Saturdays Events in November/December and in May

Successful, sustainable programs use FLL and FTC as feeder programs Detroit has some unique challenges The way schools feed into each other Transportation…always transportation An ideal setup is having high school students mentoring the middle and elementary programs, but we are not there yet

You are not expected to coach FLL or FTC on top of FRC. If you want to just check things out, you could Stop in to a Saturday session and see it Stop in to a competition as a spectator Volunteer at an event for a day Judging is an interesting experience Doing Unified Robotics in the fall has some similarities Get in touch with coaches of your feeder middle schools and schedule a robot demo to recruit for FRC

Special Olympics-affiliated robotics program Organized by King HS and run at the MEZ and DHDC Unified uses the same kits as Lego League If your students enjoyed doing Unified, they might enjoy working with elementary students to teach FLL Again, not something you’re expected to coordinate
That can be both bad and good, but mostly it is just a lot There are some lesser known aspects to FRC that are good to understand to have a smoother season

There are different kinds of events District (standard) District (third play) Regional State Championship World Championship Offseason Generally, district, state championship, and offseason events are most relevant to MEZ teams, but there are exceptions

Every team gets two district events by default; these are your standard events You play 12 matches and potentially playoffs You earn district points towards qualifying for the state championship based on your final rank, how many playoff matches you win, and any awards you earn There is a lottery for third district events; if you win you can sign up for $500 Third plays do not count towards state rankings. Your first two events count towards qualification, even if one of them is the one you got into from the lottery.

Many teams do not use the district system and instead play at one or more regionals These are higher production value but also twice as expensive as district events (you have to register for each individually) You could sign up for a regional if you wanted to, but generally these are not relevant for Michigan teams

The top 160 teams based on district points qualify for the state championship There are typically extremely few declines (zero in 2026) The event is held in Saginaw in April, and is 4x40 team events in the same arena The winners of each sub-event (called divisions) play each other for the overall champion Qualifying for the state championship is very hard, but it is doable

The top ~85 teams from Michigan qualify for the world championship Takes place in Houston, TX in late April or early May Two MEZ teams qualified last year for the first time ever Logistically, extremely difficult to make this work, but it is possible There are differing opinions on whether or not this is a good use of resources There were 20+ declines from Michigan in 2026

Many events take place on weekends from June-October Some are competitive, some are casual, some are a mix of both Good opportunity to get additional drive or pit practice, make friends, and just have fun They typically cost $250-400 per event day The Detroit City Championship is on Saturday, October 10th this year and is FREE for MEZ teams

Event registration is handled through two rounds of “preferencing”, and then an open registration period During the preferencing periods, you can make an ordered list of your preferences Each team is randomly assigned a number and then the preferences are run in order. Subsequent rounds flip the order. If you’re unlucky on the first round, you’re more likely to be lucky on the second, but often only the first round matters There are also “home events”

Every team gets one home event, which is assigned based on your zip code During the first round of preferencing, you can either opt in or opt out of your home event If you opt in, you are GUARANTEED a spot there If you opt out, you may be able to get in later through normal selection, but it’s not guaranteed

Generally, Detroit events are vastly over capacity The Renaissance (later Troy 2) event had almost 40 teams on the waitlist last year Gail tries to help us how she can but FIM has to respect the lottery order It’s highly recommended to opt in to your home event if it’s in Detroit For your second event, you will generally want to list the other Detroit event as your first and only preference, and select “allow waitlist” If it turns out you’re way down the waitlist (FIM will tell us), then you can choose a different event Your event selections are up to you, and if you want to go to a different event, you can!

There’s an “Event Change Request Form” on the FIM website during the season Fill it out if you don’t get the event you want If you end up 30th on the waitlist it won’t work out, but it doesn’t cost you anything to do You can fill out the form for multiple potential event swaps The MEZ will try to support the events we can, but if you end up very far away it may not be possible We will always support the Detroit events

Every team is supposed to volunteer 4 full human days at each district event they attend Historically, community-wide, we don’t quite hit that mark Many teams fill these roles with parents; that’s not an option for everyone There are other great sources of volunteers Colleagues from your school Responsible students (if your team is large enough) Alumni who live in the area Alumni are fantastic as they can stay involved without the commitment of mentoring We can work together to bring more volunteers into the community

These are the parts you get on kickoff day each year You always get a season-specific box, and could get more than that (next slide) Likely everyone will get some controls stuff next year because of SystemCore You’ll have to go into the dashboard at some point, generally September or October, and select the MEZ as your kickoff pickup site. Keep an eye out for FIRST Team Blasts that talk about the deadline. Always inventory your kit of parts when you get it!

You can opt out of the kit of parts chassis and the black tote If you’re doing swerve, opt out of the chassis to get a $450 AndyMark voucher The black tote contains what you need to build a KitBot, so if you want to do a KB or EveryBot, definitely keep that Otherwise, you can opt out to get a ~$200 voucher for Rev You can also pre-order additional game pieces, but at the MEZ there’s generally no need to do this Teams building elsewhere may want to consider it

There is a “virtual” kit of parts that you can access in your FIRST dashboard This contains licenses for various software products It also contains vouchers for discounted or even free stuff Often you have until mid or late May to use some of the vouchers It’s worth scrolling through and seeing if anything interests you!

You can make a 40x40 pixel avatar to represent your team at the events If you don’t, you get a default FIRST logo You can only upload this twice per season because they’re manually reviewed by a human Having an avatar adds branding and character to your team for everyone to see If you have an artist on your team, they can make one, but also now with AI it’s easy to create something better than the default

If you get grants through FIRST, you can have FIRST regrant them to any nonprofit org This is done through the FIRST dashboard If you use 313 as a fiduciary, you can have them send the money there Just make sure to do this before the end of the school year

A program that lets you get free stuff that was donated to FIRST by vendors There’s a lot of junk, but some good stuff too You get credits each year and bid on items with a “priority list” There are typically two rounds It’s worth the time to browse and make a list each year

FIRST has a page with grant opportunities Many require mentors or parents with a connection to an org, but not all It’s work checking every once in a while Just apply! You never know what will happen.

Many colleges offer FIRST-specific scholarships FIRST has a website page dedicated to this, with a searchable list This is up to your students to act on, but good to be aware of Reminder that the MEZ offers Career and College Advising as well
Every team has different motivations and values Being competitive on the field Building something cool Winning certain awards Reaching student development milestones What is meaningful to your team?

A wide range of goals are all good What matters more than your goals is that your team has similar goals, or at least some shared goals Sometimes goals conflict with each other As coaches we have a lot of influence on our students and their goals Of course, that influence has limits too Having everyone understand the team goals is important

Discuss the handout worksheet in a small group (3-4 people, at least two schools) You don’t have to fill it out if you don’t want to, but at least consider it After a few minutes we’ll share out to the larger group

documents.t: “Computer Aided Design” How pretty much everything in the world is designed, including robots Useful tool even if you aren’t a designer In FRC, by far the most common CAD program is Onshape
Perfect for FRC Works online; students don’t need powerful computers Most robots you would want to build are published publicly in Onshape Mouse highly recommended
Zoom, Pan, Rotate Measure Hide/Isolate/Section view Change configurations Find in instance list Export

More and more parts can simply be printed Easier and more precise than fabricating by hand Slow in real time, but fast in terms of human time. Print overnight for best results. Good for inspiring students The MEZ has printers you can use

Export an STL from Onshape or download it from a vendor Open it in what’s called “slicing” software Arrange it, duplicate it, etc, and then slice it Load the file onto the USB or SD card, and run your print!

CAD and 3D printing are extremely useful tools for your build season Being able to navigate Onshape documents will save you a lot of time when assembling your robot Many parts need to be 3D printed, even for Kitbot/Everybot builds Use Onshape to export and print parts, or find or design your own upgrades!

AndyMark - the original; solid, entry-level parts Rev Robotics - advanced parts but reliability issues in recent years West Coast Products - typically the “best” or most competitive parts, but very expensive Cross the Road Electronics - MI-based, sells electrical components; partnered with WCP ThriftyBot - growing quickly; sometimes has good parts at lower prices

Makes sure crimps are extremely tight Otherwise, brownout and fire risk Never lift by the cables Everyone will do this by default so make a point of warning people One of the easiest ways to simply purchase a competitive advantage
Robot’s on/off switch Make sure terminals are extremely tight Otherwise, brownout and fire risk Make it visible and accessible to field staff

Sits between your battery and everything else Has snap-action breakers that break, and then reset, if there’s too much current Three main variants PDP, or power distribution panel PDP 2 PDH, or power distribution hub

Two types of motor Brushed: old, less efficient but fine, cheap Brushless: better in every way but expensive Two main sizes of motor CIM-class: big motors Smaller motors (no generic class name) Three main brands of motors CIMs - brushed but good enough, and free Rev NEOs - “normal”, vortex, and mini (550) WCP Kraken - normal and mini

SparkMax By far the most common at the MEZ Exists separately from the motor Spark Flex SparkMax but for the Neo Vortex Separate part but docks with the motor TalonFX For Krakens Built in so you don’t think much about it
Also called IMUs, which stands for Inertial Measurement Unit Measures rotation of the robot Critical for swerve drive Helpful for programming Several common models May be built into SystemCore

Measure rotation of a motor or mechanism Built in to modern motors, so they’re easy to use Two main types: relative and absolute Relative Encoders Know how many times they’ve spun around Great for things like flywheels that repeat positions Absolute Encoders Know exactly where they are Great for things where only the position matters Swerve steering The position of an arm
Sometimes you want extra power slots for small items CTRE VRM REV Mini-PDH
Sometimes you want extra power slots for small items CTRE VRM REV Mini-PDH
The software library used to program FRC robots Created at Worcester Polytechnic Institute You’ll need to download it each year, which we’ll do now

Search for “frc zero to robot” Find the FIRST Robotics Competition Documentation Click “Step 2: Installing Software” Click “WPILib Installation Guide” and follow the directions for the WPILib Installer

Used for configuring Rev hardware, specifically SparkMaxes They need CAN IDs, but you can also change other settings and even drive them Search for “Rev Hardware Client” Click the installation link and install the software

Software wins matches In 2024: 528 teams built a kitbot 25% of points were scored in auto Software, along with driving, is what differentiates teams Competitive teams automate tasks in teleop as well, such as aiming
Moving an elevator to an exact position Setting a flywheel to an exact speed Auto aiming at a goal Rumbling the controller when the robot successfully picks up a game piece

Work on wiring up a complete electrical board Use the Rev Hardware Client to ID your motors Also use the hardware client to get a motor to spin Head to the programming station as a team to make and deploy code changes

Team supervision is required, but not MEZ supervision or machine shop certification Please stock and label your own tools You can borrow things you rarely use, but please make an effort to return them Check and put away the tools on your table after each day

Check your tools at the end of EVERY day!

Everything the MEZ does is a tradeoff in terms of what to use our resources on More technical mentors vs more materials for teams vs robot transportation etc We want teams to be aware of what we can offer We also request teams respect our guidelines and requests If you have suggestions for improving things, please speak up I promise I listen to and consider every suggestion - even if I don’t end up doing it

Robotics Fall workshops Detroit City Championship Unified Robotics MEZ build season Student summer camp Teacher/mentor workshops Other programs Career and College Advising Future Ready Scholars One-off opportunities such as career days, etc

Food every day Access to technical mentors and machine shop supervision Parts and raw materials Access to tools and machines Access to a serviceable practice field and sufficient game pieces Robot transportation to and from almost all events Technical assistance at events, within resources Community with a large number of other schools and teams Partnership with other Detroit organizations such as DHDC Bus support for DPSCD teams A table for your team where you can leave your stuff Probably more…
As part of the community, we also have some things we request from you

Treat everyone with respect Cooperate with MEZ staff when they have a request Help clean the facility when asked Clean up after yourselves every day In food areas (lunch/dinner, and the break room) In the machine shop or common work areas On the floor where you’re working (shavings, parts, debris, etc) Move tables as needed Follow all safety rules Safety glasses Ears unobstructed Loose hair/clothing/accessories/etc tied back Please, no singing/whistling/clapping/loud music/etc

Serve as the supervisor and responsible adult for all your team members This means enforcing the expectations as needed The MEZ cannot supervise 100 students - we are relying on you Legal responsibility for your team members Students should not be at the MEZ before you arrive or after you leave Please ensure they are gone before departing each day Serve as the leader of your team Take responsibility for your build - MEZ mentors are here to assist, but not to lead your team Come with a plan each day that doesn’t wholly rely on MEZ staff Work to engage your students and minimize the number in the break room Make an effort to submit bus requests by the deadline and minimize the number of cancellations/last-minute changes

Your drivetrain is, by far, the most important part of your robot. Many years, simply having a strong, well-driven drivetrain is enough to make you a highly competitive team. There are two main drivetrain options: tank and swerve. The best choice varies by team and depends on your resources.

The starter drivetrain Three wheels on each side; turns by driving each side at a different speed Powered by two motors for each side Simple to build and extremely reliable Comes free with your season registration unless you opt out Lets you focus on scoring mechanisms

A more advanced option, and more competitive Four “modules”, each with one wheel, one in each corner Powered by four drive motors and four steer motors (eight total) A lot easier than it used to be, but far from trivial Expensive - assume $1200+ for modules, plus eight motors and controllers If you want swerve, get it working in the fall. It is not recommended to switch to swerve during a build season.

This is your first year You did not have a week or more of drive practice last season Your mechanisms weren’t fully tuned You don’t plan on having team meetings before January You don’t have $2000+ to spare You’re just not sure if you want to commit

You finished early last year and got drive practice time in Your mechanisms worked and scored successfully The biggest thing holding you back from scoring more was not being able to move sideways You have time to build and test it in the fall You have at least $2000 allocated for it There is nothing wrong with choosing tank. You will never regret a season because your robot didn’t have swerve.
The AndyMark kit chassis comes in the kit of parts each year The cost is included in your registration fee so you won’t have to pay anything

You will have to pick a vendor and purchase modules. Historically, MEZ teams have used Rev, but we do not recommend this going forward. For 26-27, the MEZ will recommend West Coast Products Swerve X2 variants, but other vendors such as Swerve Drive Specialties are reasonable. Make sure whatever you pick is compatible with the motors you have. If you go swerve, remember to opt out of the kit chassis.

Bumpers seem like an afterthought but they are a critical robot component If your bumpers are out of spec, you will not be able to play matches The rules change a little bit year to year and the specifics matter a lot Even so, the gist is you need foam protecting most or all of your robot frame

The MEZ will do Bumper Day again in 2027 Friends come in and help mass-produce bumper components for every team This includes fabric, foam, wood backing, and numbers Try to attend, but either way, take bumpers seriously and allocate time in advance towards building them!
Keep it simple!!! Identify your needs & set goals Lean on your community Expand & scale when you’re ready
Identify your needs Students? Mentors? Areas of Interest (Mechanical, Programming, Design, Business, etc.) Set goals Students Entry-level goal: 2-3 students Mentors Entry-level goal: 1 mentor

Lean on your community School Every event is an opportunity (Back to School nights, Level Ups, sporting events, STEM nights, assemblies) Staff -> potential mentors - not just teachers! Academic Interventionists, Clerical Staff, etc. Work with staff to recruit students Work with students to recruit students Family & Friends - Introduce them to FIRST Share updates! In person, social media, etc. Invite them to events Show them it’s accessible to support (once a week, etc.)

Social media / website Supporting FLL & FTC Entry-level: One school, One day Can be helpful to recruit students and sometimes even mentors! Creating new opportunities for recruitment & awareness Speaking at PDs Admin sending emails

Why are you raising money? This dictates how much money you need A DPSCD MEZ team could probably operate indefinitely without fundraising But, if a team wants to be very competitive, it can get expensive quickly

There are four main ways teams raise money Grants Sponsorships Fundraising Team dues Different situations favor different methods Grants and sponsorships tend to be higher $/hour overall, but are high variance
Working concessions Selling things in school Doing a gofundme What else?
Haas grant FIRST grants page Ask AI? Haven’t tried but I bet it works What else?

Companies strongly prefer sponsoring organizations they have a connection to For corporations, that typically means if an employee is affiliated with the team Reach out to all of your parents If they work for an automaker, that’s fantastic (GM is the best) Even if not, their company may be willing to give $500 Companies that focus on community are good options Credit unions, car dealerships, etc You can go door to door with your students and solicit companies What else?

Mostly a matter of pulling up a diagram and following it Care and precision is helpful Pay attention to wire gauge Pay attention to which color of wire goes where Black to black and red to red Yellow to yellow and green to green

Gauge or AWG (American Wire Gauge) is the size of wire A smaller number means bigger wire In FRC, the most common gauges are: 6 for battery cable 12 for motor wires 18-22 for light power and signal wires There are always exceptions
One of the biggest failure points for robots Wagos/lever nuts Anderson crimps Molex crimps Soldering Care and aggressive testing are more important than which method you use
Designed to cut metallic wire without quickly getting dull. Often combined with wire strippers in a single tool.
Designed to pull the ends of sheathing off of a run of wire.
Crushes some kind of connector onto a wire. Can be generic, but also there are many designed for certain kinds of crimps.

Flush cutter blades are off-center so that they can cut something flush with another surface Non-flush ziptie cuts are surprisingly dangerous The MEZ will buy a large stock of these before the season Safety glasses are very important - the cut piece will sometimes go flying

Short circuits, or shorts, happen when there’s a connection where there shouldn’t be Electricity can take a shorter path than intended, which often overloads an item Main causes: Connecting the wrong things to each other A loose strand of wire sticking out of a connector Debris on electrical components

Single-use circuit breaker If there’s too much current, it literally breaks the circuit, in this case by burning Unlike snap-action breakers, once a fuse burns, it must be physically replaced If you don’t fix the short, the replacement will immediately burn out too

Cut short-but-workable sections of wires of each different gauge Strip both ends of each wire Connect your wires together with wire nuts - Wagos for big, off-brand for small Make sure to tug test your connections Disconnect the wires Put one end of each wire into your PDP/PDH Make sure to tug test your connections Disconnect the wires from your PDP/PDH Add crimps to your wires Make sure to tug test your crimps Use a couple zip ties (on anything) and then cut them flush with a flush cutter
